# C A U T E R I U M.

<margin>15.</margin>
Therefore, pus is blood corrupted in the very part where the wound is, and it is the effect of a digestion that has been corrupted there. To have corrupted the integrity, continuity, and digestion of the parts, and finally to have converted blood into pus, is what has been esteemed in the *Schools* to be the same as having averted <term>Catarrhs</term> <gloss>downward-flowing discharges</gloss>: whether by extracting through the opening of the cautery an excremental humor (which otherwise had threatened to settle upon a noble part) from the head, from whence they all originally seek their *Catarrhs*: or whether or not there be a consensus between the head and the wounded part; for it is the same thing, provided the wounded skin is kept open. Whether that excremental humor be blood, or becomes pus, or <term>sanies</term> <gloss>thin, watery discharge</gloss>, it is the same, provided the world is circumvented through the worn-out terms of Catarrh, precaution, derivation, revulsion, and <term>fontanella</term> <gloss>an artificial ulcer or seton for drainage</gloss>. For I observe a year-old infant, now teething, suffering from fever, mouth foam, and ceaseless saliva. And finally, there are gripings and stools of a yellowish-green color. At least that tooth is a part of the head: therefore, diarrhea will be a Catarrh of the head. But what is the consensus of an erupting tooth, or of a swollen gum, with the intestine? Or what is its power of generating, of sending a Catarrh from the infant’s stomach to the head? And thence into the *Ileon*? By what right will a vapor distilled from the stomach become greenish bile in the head? Has the workshop of bile perhaps migrated to the head since the beginning of life? Could a cautery (if the infant were capable of enduring it) drive the porraceous <note>resembling leeks, often referring to a green, bilious discharge</note> diarrhea into itself? And compensate for several pounds of porraceous bile with a few tiny drops of pus? Why does the infant’s stomach manufacture a Catarrh because of a toothache? Why is it sent into the intestine, and not to the aching tooth? Does the reader not yet see that diarrhea is not a Catarrh? But rather that the indignant *Archeus* <gloss>the internal vital agent or governing principle of the body</gloss> anywhere, being ready in the intestine to transmute the alimentary chyme into excrements, which are thought by the *Schools* to be bile, phlegm, etc. If, therefore, diarrhea is not a Catarrh, and the indignant *Archeus* can 

<column-break/>

transmute whatever he likes into a harmful liquid, provided the gum is afflicted, could he not exonerate himself in every direction through established emunctories <gloss>cleansing or excretory organs</gloss>? And not wait for the skin to be opened by a caustic? Ah, cruel dullness, has it made the *Schools* behave fiercely toward mortals born of the same stock?
<margin>16.</margin>
For they do not consider that, in women and obese people, the fleshy membrane around the ordinary sites of the cautery is mere lard to a thickness of at least two fingers, yet it is to these persons that more frequent and more beneficial cauteries are recommended. Wherefore, the base of the *fontanella* will scarcely be in the middle of the fat. 
<margin>17.</margin>
There is therefore no path by which the evil, fictitious humor—proscribed as a *Catarrh*—may rush from the brain, or from between the cranium and the skin, through the middle of the fat. But what, finally, is that solitary humor, which, having been proscribed by its own fault by the part sending it, descending unmixed through the substance of the fat, degenerates into pus? If it were an exhalation of vapors from the stomach, why would it not be more frequent in the young, and those with warm stomachs, than in the weak, the old, and the cold? In what way will this water, distilled from vapor, put on the form of pus? How will it hasten through the brain, the meninges, and the cranium to find the opening made by the cautery, so that it may flow out and be purged only by that path? Why does the vapor not fly off into the air a hundred times before it reaches the place designated by the compliant cautery? How will water climbing from the stomach be blood and the matter of pus? How will blood (the matter of pus, according to *Galen*) be the matter of *Catarrh*? Why must blood be reduced to the series of bad humors, which, not yet contaminated, is dispensed by nature to the wounded place? Why, once a wound is made, will nature cease to disturb the condemned matter through and into its accustomed places? For once the skin is opened at the pleasure of the healer, will it become ignorant of deviations? Or has it perhaps labored only to find an exit somewhere? And having done so, will it henceforth come to the bidding of the one inflicting the wound? Thus these four are false,

<summary>Van Helmont argues that the discharge from medical cauteries is not the drainage of harmful humors or "catarrh" from the head, but rather the corruption of healthy blood caused by the artificial wound itself. He criticizes the medical establishment for ignoring anatomical realities, such as the layer of fat that prevents deep drainage, and dismisses the theory of catarrh as a fictitious explanation for vital processes he attributes to the Archeus.</summary>
<keywords>cautery, fontanella, catarrh, Archeus, pus, medical theory, Galen, humors, anatomy</keywords>
